title: Prudential Regulation Authority Business Plan 2026/27
summary: The PRA published its 2026/27 Business Plan outlining regulatory priorities including embedding liquidity reporting for insurers, implementing Basel III reforms (finalized January 2026), and responding to faster bank runs experienced in 2023. The document confirms approximately 140 staff headcount reduction and a shift to two-year Periodic Summary Meetings cycles for supervised firms.
key_points: Basel III implementation completed in January 2026; full embedding proceeds through 2026/27 without increasing overall capital requirements for banks
Simplified capital regime for small domestic banks will be fully in place from January 2027
PRA is taking forward work on bank liquidity rules responding to faster bank runs experienced in 2023, primarily in the US
PRA regulates 1,254 firms: 686 deposit-takers and 568 insurers of all types
Operational incident reporting and third-party relationship reporting requirements being implemented jointly with FCA
Material headcount reduction of approximately 140 staff this year, with savings reinvested in systems and technology
Chief Executive Sam Woods' term concludes in June 2026; Katharine Braddick to succeed
why_it_matters: The PRA's regulatory agenda affects capital requirements, liquidity standards, and operational resilience requirements for UK banks and insurers. Changes to bank liquidity rules (responding to 2023 US bank run dynamics) and implementation of Basel III standards will influence how UK financial institutions manage balance sheets and meet regulatory thresholds. The shift to two-year PSM cycles reduces supervisory burden for firms.

It notes commitment to supporting sustainable economic growth while maintaining prudential standards. This is background regulatory context rather than direct macro catalyst information.
market_structure_context: The document discusses regulatory frameworks (Basel III capital rules, liquidity standards, ring-fencing regime) that shape market structure for UK banks and insurers. It does not address market trading dynamics, liquidity in secondary markets, or market microstructure.
